The key is understanding CSS stacking contexts. `root>low` has `z-index: 1` and creates a new stacking context because it's positioned. All its children (including `root>low>inner` with `z-index: 999`) are confined to that stacking context. `root>high` has `z-index: 2` in the root stacking context. Since the parent stacking context `root>low` (z-index 1) is below `root>high` (z-index 2), the entire `root>low` tree paints below `root>high`, regardless of the child's higher z-index value. The provided information explicitly confirms this: "the smaller z-index still wins here because this node's z-index 999 is scoped to the stacking context of root>low, and that whole context paints below root>high".

ANSWER: root>high
